newsitem.title: UK: Britain pessimistic on lifting of beef export ban.
newsitem.headline: Britain pessimistic on lifting of beef export ban.

text.p: British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg said on Wednesday he did not expect an early lifting of the export ban on British beef even though his country had complied with European Union demands for the tackling of "mad cow" disease.

Hogg said he thought scientists would be unable, at least in the short term, to resolve a key issue in the mad cow crisis -- the question of whether bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) can be passed from cow to calf.
Asked in a BBC radio interview whether he believed British farmers would soon be able to send their cattle abroad again, Hogg said: "I am not confident".

Britain triggered the mad cow crisis last March when it said it may be possible for people to contract the human form of BSE, a fatal brain disease called CJD, from eating beef. The EU reacted by imposing a worldwide export ban on British beef.

Hogg said Britain, which in December agreed to the slaughter of an extra 100,000 cattle susceptible to the disease, has fulfilled the terms of an agreement reached at an EU summit in Florence, Italy for a lifting of the ban.

"We are now entitled to look to the Europeans to fulfil their side of the bargain but...it is difficult to persuade them to do that for a variety of reasons," Hogg said. He said the main reason was internal pressures on other EU governments from farming and consumer lobbies and from the fact that beef sales had plunged in their countries.
"It therefore makes them less willing to deliver that which they agreed to do at Florence," Hogg, who later on Wednesday is to address the annual meeting of Britain's National Farmers Union, said.

Asked when it would be clear whether maternal transmission of mad cow disease could take place, Hogg said: "My own bet is the scientists will not come up at least within the near future with a definitive answer."
He said there were two possibilities -- one that the disease could be passed from cow to calf and the other that susceptibility to catching it from contaminated feedstuffs was transmissable.
In either event, it was clear that maternal transmission was at a very low level, Hogg said.
Scientists believe that thousands of cases of BSE in British cows resulted from the incorporation of pig entrails in the feed of cattle, natural herbivores.
New controls have been put in place to stop this, but if the possibility of the disease being passed on genetically has raised fears that this might not be enough to eradicate it.
